# HELP WANTED: Scientists Seeking Senior Dogs To Unlock the Secrets of Aging

Image: Dr. Paola Cuevas

By Dr. Paola CuevasUpdated on October 20, 2026

Share

Ask us a question in the comments

Image: HELP WANTED: Scientists Seeking Senior Dogs To Unlock the Secrets of Aging

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

That is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is currently looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

* * *

### Why Rapamycin?

Rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

The interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

The Dog Aging Project’s TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

Image

### It’s Not Just About Lifespan

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

Lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

Those are not the same thing.

Living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

### Which Dogs Can Participate?

The current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:

  * Be aged 7 years or older

  * Weigh 44 to 120 pounds

  * Be spayed or neutered

  * Be in overall good health

  * Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation

  * Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

For families who decide to participate, it is important to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

Image

* * *

### Why Dogs Are So Valuable To Aging Research

When it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

The recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

There's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a big deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

But this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

Aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

### All Dogs Can Contribute

Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesn’t mean they can’t contribute to canine aging research.

The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

It’s important to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

Image: senior dog lying on dog bedImage Credit: Yobab, Shutterstock

* * *

### There’s So Much to Learn About Aging Dogs

When it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

That's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

For owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

Debbie Doppelt, a New Yorker with a rare form of lung cancer, turned to China in early 2025 for sunvozertinib, a drug targeting her tumor’s mutation, after being ineligible for U.S. clinical trials and lacking FDA-approved options. The drug, developed by Chinese firm Dizal Pharmaceutical, was approved in China in 2023 and is set for U.S. distribution in 2027 via AstraZeneca. China has rapidly become a biotech leader, offering faster and more flexible clinical trials compared to the U.S., drawing international patients and investment. In response, the U.S. launched Operation TrialBlazer to streamline approvals. Some U.S. lawmakers push for curbing collaborations with Chinese biotech, while others advocate for pragmatic, global cooperation in fighting diseases. Inspired by his mother’s experience, Max Doppelt created an AI-driven platform to help patients find clinical trials. The situation highlights challenges in U.S. drug regulations and the growing prominence of China in global drug innovation, underscoring the life-or-death stakes for patients and the need for international collaboration in medical advancements.

"I think I've been pretty successful at having, actually, an amazing three years," she said. "In some ways a better three years, with all of it, than the three years before, because you're so appreciative of everything."
Doppelt's parents were Holocaust survivors. "They were always saying: 'This piece of bread tastes so good! Do you know what it is to be hungry?'"
Doppelt has done well on the drug. About 19 months after starting  it, her cancer was still mostly kept at bay, with the help of a few radiation treatments and dose adjustments.
AstraZeneca's plans to widely distribute sunvozertinib would mean no more trips to China. But Max had few illusions that the drug would work for his mom forever.
"She has a metastasizing cancer that will learn to bypass the drug," he said. "At that point we'll be dependent on the latest and greatest therapies. If they happen to be in China, I'll do everything in our power to go there."
At his Upper East Side apartment one recent afternoon, Max examined the current clinical trial outlook for his mother. He pulled up her profile on the app and scrolled down a list scoring available trial sites according to their fit and proximity.
"This one looks good," he said, pointing to a clinical trial for firmonertinib, a drug China approved in 2021 that's under study in the United States and elsewhere.
CAR-T therapy is another possibility, particularly a variety that the University of Colorado has developed to boost patients' immunological attack on mutations like the ones driving Doppelt's cancer.
But Kyle Concannon, a leader of the Colorado research team, said regulatory uncertainty has slowed his progress. As new tools enable sophisticated measures of things like toxicity and tissue distribution, they add time, cost and risk to the therapy's development. These technologies may be better at detecting possible harms, "which is good," Concannon said, "but the alternative to a new medicine, with a natural disease like lung cancer, is the individuals will die from their disease."
Max Doppelt and other patient advocates, while pushing for faster FDA processes, don't want to rule out more Chinese medicine runs.
"When drugs are approved in China but not in the U.S., of course we will deploy the China option where necessary," said Marcia Horn, CEO of the nonprofit International Cancer Advocacy Network. "Lives depend on it."
Max would prefer to see the drugs his mother needs developed in the United States. But he, too, opposes any effort to freeze out the Chinese biotech industry.

Autologous patient-specific tumor antigen response
Medical intervention

Autologous patient-specific tumor antigen response
Specialty | Oncology
Autologous patient-specific tumor antigen response (apSTAR) technology is a new cancer treatment procedure being developed by IMULAN BioTherapeutics, LLC and Veterinary Cancer Therapeutics, LLC for comparative oncology.

Also known as laser-assisted immunotherapy, apSTAR is an experimental cancer treatment for solid tumors that uses an autologous vaccine-like approach to stimulate immune responses. Specifically, laser-assisted immunotherapy combines laser-induced in situ tumor devitalization with an immunoadjuvant for local immunostimulation.
## Principles of apSTAR

The two principles underlying apSTAR are: local destruction of tumor by means of a laser combined with a photo-absorbing dye and stimulated immune response due to the application of an immunoadjuvant, but also due to increases in antigen accessibility caused by the destruction of the tumor. Both elements of this protocol are crucial. Since this method independently triggers the immune response in each individual, it does not depend upon cross reactivity in the expression of tumor-specific antigen between hosts (as is required in conventional antibody immunotherapy and vaccination.)
## Trials

Veterinary Cancer Therapeutics, LLC, a subsidiary of IMULAN BioTherapeutics, LLC, is in exploratory trials for canine osteosarcoma, canine melanoma, canine and feline fibrosarcoma, and several other forms of cancer.

DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25405)
【turn1106academia24】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 4 days ago; 
Title: DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial
Authors: Vanessa Rodriguez, Brieuc Lehmann, Karla Diaz-Ordaz
Date: Sun Oct 18 17:03:30 2026

Randomized clinical trials are essential for evaluating interventions, yet average treatment effects can obscure treatment effect heterogeneity, making conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) a natural target. However, restrictive eligibility criteria and differential trial participation can limit the generalizability of these effects to broader target populations. Building on existing DR-Learners, we develop the gDR-Learner for generalizing RCT CATEs to a target population, using cross-fitted machine-learning nuisance estimation. We derive excess-risk bounds in which nuisance errors enter only as products, showing that the estimator achieves oracle-rate convergence despite slower individual nuisance estimation. The variables needed to generalize are rarely measured across the entire target population. We therefore extend the methods to two settings with incomplete covariate information: when certain covariates are measured only in the trial (e.g., biomarkers), and covariates driving trial participation measured only in a subsample of the target population, such as a representative cohort or registry. We construct weighted conformal prediction intervals for individual treatment effects, accounting for covariate shift between the trial and target population. In simulations, the gDR-Learner achieved the lowest estimation error when all covariates were observed relative to standard T- and DR-Learners and an inverse-probability-weighted T-Learner, and also outperformed the latter under incomplete covariate observation. We illustrate the methods by reanalyzing the Coronary Artery Surgery Study, examining treatment effect heterogeneity by prior myocardial infarction and baseline ejection fraction.

PRET is a few-shot system for pan-cancer recognition without example training (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25054)
【turn1106academia25】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 5 days ago; 
Title: PRET is a few-shot system for pan-cancer recognition without example training
Authors: Yi Li, Ziyu Ning, Tianqi Xiang, Qixiang Zhang, Zhihao Lin, Min Yi, Feiyan Feng, Baozhen Zeng, Xuexia Qian, Lu Sun, Jiace Qin, Ling Xiang, Chao Fan, Tian Qin, Qian Wang, Xiu-Wu Bian, Kun-Hsing Yu, Kang Zhang, Qingling Zhang, Xiaomeng Li
Date: Sun Oct 18 06:48:27 2026

Pathological examination stands as the cornerstone in cancer diagnosis, impacting millions worldwide annually. With the shortage of pathologists globally, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged rapidly to automate the diagnostics process. However, conventional AI models require substantial labeled data for each disease, posing huge challenges in scalability and practicality. Therefore, we introduce PRET (pan-cancer recognition without examples training), a few-shot system to achieve flexible, scalable, and effective cancer recognition across diverse organs, hospitals and tasks without training. Evaluated on 23 international benchmarks comprising 4,484 whole-slide images, our method outperforms existing approaches across 20 tasks, achieving over 97% area under the curve on 15 benchmarks with a maximum improvement of 36.76%. Notably, PRET delivers clinical-grade diagnostic performance in lymph node metastasis detection using only eight slide examples, outperforming 11 pathologists. By offering a flexible and cost-effective solution for pan-cancer recognition, PRET paves the way for accessible and equitable AI-based pathology systems, particularly benefiting minority populations and underserved regions.

Title: Evidence-informed dynamic modelling and intervention prioritisation in diabetic bone marrow
Authors: Paolo Madeddu
Date: Sat Oct 17 14:48:31 2026

Aims. Fragmented understanding of how diabetes disrupts interconnected bone marrow niches has hindered integrated strategies to restore function. Building on a previous static network, we developed a dynamic model to simulate intervention responses. Methods. The investigator and ChatGPT dialogued to extract evidence from a frozen corpus and develop the model. A Python implementation extended Boolean logic to three ordinal levels (0, 1 and 2) representing biological states and, where applicable, intervention strength. Under high metabolic stress, 15 interventions were assessed at three strengths and four with binary settings; 171 pairs were tested at maximal strength. A domain balanced score (0 to100) integrated favourable and adverse changes. Staged simulations assessed withdrawal; regulatory constraints on recovery after metabolic stress reduction were examined separately. Results. Endothelial reactive oxygen species (ROS) suppression achieved the highest score among 19 single interventions (24.2), improving three functional domains. Endothelial protein kinase B (Akt) augmentation scored 15.2 (two domains); oncostatin M (OSM) blockade and haematopoietic 66 kDa SHC transforming protein 1 (p66Shc) loss each scored 13.6 (two domains). ROS suppression combined with either OSM blockade or p66Shc loss scored 37.9, (five domains). No pair restored all functions under high stress. Benefits of ROS suppression, Akt augmentation and ROS and OSM blockade disappeared after withdrawal. Reducing metabolic stress led to variable scores (range 4.5 to 100), increasing mainly with restored endothelial function, followed by progenitor recovery and interruption of inflammatory and adipocyte stromal signalling. Conclusions. These simulations offer a rule based framework for investigating diabetic marrow recovery. Experimental studies must establish whether it can guide targeted therapy.
